summary: Jesus tells of a widow who kept coming to an unjust judge until he gave her justice, to teach that His people should always pray and not lose heart.
key_insight: Luke gives the point before the story begins: “men always ought to pray and not lose heart.” But Jesus ends with a question about us, not about God: “when the Son of Man comes, will He really find faith on the earth?” God’s faithfulness is certain; ours is what is in question.
story: Jesus told His disciples a parable to show that “men always ought to pray and not lose heart.”
In a certain city, He said, there was a judge “who did not fear God nor regard man.” A widow in that city kept coming to him with one plea: “Get justice for me from my adversary.”
For a while he refused. But afterward he said to himself, “Though I do not fear God nor regard man, yet because this widow troubles me I will avenge her, lest by her continual coming she weary me.”

“Hear what the unjust judge said,” the Lord told them. “And shall God not avenge His own elect who cry out day and night to Him, though He bears long with them? I tell you that He will avenge them speedily.”
Then He asked, “Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, will He really find faith on the earth?”

scene.label: Widows
scene.text: With no husband to speak for her and often no property of her own, a widow had few defenders. The Law placed her under God’s own protection: “If you afflict them in any way, and they cry at all to Me, I will surely hear their cry” (Exodus 22:23).

scene.label: A judge who feared no one
scene.text: Israel’s judges were told to judge justly and take no bribe (Deuteronomy 16:18–19). This one admits that he answers neither to God nor to public opinion. A poor widow had nothing to offer him except her persistence.

scene.label: “Weary me”
scene.text: The word literally means to strike under the eye, a term from boxing; Paul uses it of disciplining his own body (1 Corinthians 9:27). The judge may be half joking that she will give him a black eye, or mean that she will wear him down. Either way, he gives in to be rid of her.

scene.label: Night and day
scene.text: Luke has already introduced another widow who “served God with fastings and prayers night and day”: Anna, who met the infant Jesus in the temple (Luke 2:36–38).

scene.label: Bears long
scene.text: God’s delay is patience, not neglect. Peter later writes that the Lord “is longsuffering toward us, not willing that any should perish” (2 Peter 3:9).

witnesses.luke: Only Luke tells this parable, and he follows it at once with another on prayer, the Pharisee and the tax collector. Luke shows Jesus at prayer more than any other Gospel writer, and here he ties prayer to the end of the age: the parable comes right after Jesus’ teaching on the day of the Son of Man (17:22–37).

seeing.reveals: Jesus pictures the Father as the opposite of the unjust judge: He hears His own, He will act, and His slowness is patience. Jesus Himself is the Son of Man who will come looking for faith.
seeing.living: Keep bringing the same plea for justice, and do not lose heart when the answer is slow. Persistent prayer is not wearing down an unwilling God; it is faith that will not give up on a willing one.
seeing.ponder: What prayer have you stopped praying because the answer was slow, and what would it mean to bring it to God again?

preaching.big_idea: God is nothing like the unjust judge, so keep praying and do not lose heart.
outline: A widow who would not stop (2–5)
A God who is nothing like the judge (6–8a)
A question for those who wait (8b)
preaching.watch_for: The parable argues from the lesser to the greater: if a judge who fears no one gives in to a stranger, how much more will God answer His own elect? The closing question ties prayer to the coming of the Son of Man, the subject of 17:22–37.
related_other: Revelation 6:9–11 · The martyrs cry, “How long, O Lord?”
